transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-12-08 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Ethan (Redwood SE), Carlos (Nimbus Head of Platform), Priya (ML Eng), Ben (Infra)

Summary:
Quick sync on POC results, focused on capacity planning for Redwood Dedicated: clarifying steady-state concurrency, expected burst patterns, autoscaling policy parameters (min/max nodes, cooldowns), and options for a burst pool / pre-warm to avoid cold starts. Agreed next steps: Redwood to send revised sizing scenarios and benchmark plan; Nimbus to share anonymized traffic profiles; schedule security deep-dive.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: hey everyone thanks for carving out the time, um today we wanna focus on sizing and the autoscale bits — make sure the Dedicated POC matches what you see in prod.
[00:18] Carlos: thanks Maya, yeah we've been running the test harness over the last week, saw some interesting spikes friday night that led to queueing, so curious about how Redwood recommends handling burst vs steady.
[00:32] Ethan: yeah cool, and just to set context, our typical approach is to size for steady throughput plus a small burst pool and then autoscale between. we can also do scheduled scale-ups if you have predictable windows.
[00:46] Priya: quick data point from our side — steady state is around 120 rps for short prompts (~60-80 tokens), but peakhour can hit 900 rps for a 10-15 minute window. those are from the client-side logs, unfiltered.
[01:02] Ben: and latency SLO is 200-250ms p50 for the frontend. p95 can be higher but we want p99 below 1s ideally.
[01:18] Maya: ok that's helpful. so two scenarios: scenario A steady at 120 rps, scenario B transient burst to 900 rps. Ethan, do you want to talk about how we convert rps to GPU capacity?
[01:30] Ethan: sure -- quick note, numbers will change based on model choice and token length. for the billed model in the POC (redwood-rt-7b-ish), we typically see X tokens/sec per A10-ish GPU under our batching defaults; with 60 tokens average it maps to roughly 40-60 requests/sec per GPU for low-latency config. for burst sizing we recommend maintaining a small hot pool (2-3 nodes) and a burst pool that can spin up to handle a 8x increase.
[01:58] Carlos: when you say spin up, what's the time to scale? we saw 90s of queueing in one test.
[02:05] Ethan: cold node boot is usually 60-120s depending on image pulls and kv-cache warmup; that's why pre-warm or a burst pool is important. you can configure a minimum hot pool to keep X replicas always warm. also we support a warmup flow that reduces cold-start pain by seeding the KV cache.
[02:25] Priya: is the KV cache the same as the KV-cache in the docs? i saw a doc but sometimes it's written k v cash in auto transcripts.
[02:31] Ethan: yeah that's the same, kv cache — it keeps the attention cache hot per session. if you lose it, the first few tokens are slower.
[02:39] Ben: from infra view — we prefer scheduled scale for our nightly batch so we don't have to rely on reactive autoscale. is that supported?
[02:45] Maya: absolutely, you can define scheduled policies in Dedicated: scale to N at time T for duration D. that pairs well with autoscale thresholds.
[02:53] Priya: can you run through an example policy? like min, target, max and the cooldowns?
[02:58] Ethan: example: min hot pool 2 nodes, target based on CPU/gpu queue depth threshold of 70% triggers add-one, cooldown 120s, max 12 nodes. for the burst pool, we set min 0, warm-prewarm 2 kept in standby for instant availability and then allow scale to 20 nodes for a large event. that's one pattern.
[03:22] Carlos: 20 nodes seems big, but if each node is sane throughput maybe needed. can you express in tokens/s or rps so i can map it to our telemetry?
[03:30] Ethan: yes, we'll put a spreadsheet but ballpark: with our current model config and batching, one GPU ~50 rps for 60-token average; so 20 nodes ~1k rps. however quantization or different instance types (A100/H100) will change that.
[03:46] Priya: are there any auto-batching knobs we should tune? we saw tail latency increase when one heavy prompt hit.
[03:52] Ethan: you can tune max batch size and max latency per batch. lowering max batch size reduces tail latency but increases cost. we can set adaptive batching thresholds per route as well.
[04:06] Ben: how do we handle model variants for fallback? for example if H100 capacity limited, can traffic go to a slightly cheaper variant without dropping requests?
[04:14] Maya: yes, smart routing lets you define fallbacks: route to variant B in lower tier or different region. that is in the rollout policy. failover can be automatic or manual.
[04:24] Carlos: one thing we noticed — in our friday spike the queue length triggered, but the autoscaler only added nodes after sustained pressure ~3m. is there a way to be more aggressive?
[04:33] Ethan: yes, you can lower the scale threshold and cooldown, or enable predictive scaling based on recent patterns. predictive scaling needs traffic history — we can help with that once you share traces.
[04:45] Priya: predictive scaling sounds useful. how does it impact cost?
[04:48] Ethan: predictive reduces cold-starts but may keep more capacity idle occasionally; for short unpredictable spikes it can be cheaper than having a large always-on pool, but depends on your duty cycle. we'll model both in the sizing sheet.
[05:02] Carlos: let's talk about burst pricing and how the billing looks if we add a hot pool + burst pool.
[05:08] Maya: pricing for Dedicated is reserved baseline plus variable usage if you exceed reserved nodes; burst pool nodes can be billed at a different rate if using on-demand capacity. i'll put the delta in the pricing sheet.
[05:16] Ben: any recommended defaults for cooldowns and scale steps? our current infra autoscaler is pretty conservative.
[05:21] Ethan: default we use: cool-down 120s, scale step +1 or +25% depending on cluster size, evaluation window 60s. for aggressive setups we do 30s cooldown and scale +2 steps. but watch oscillation.
[05:34] Priya: question about pre-warm: does pre-warm reserve GPU memory for kv-cache or just keep containers ready?
[05:39] Ethan: pre-warm keeps instances running and seeds the KV cache with representative sessions; that uses GPU memory. it means the first request won't pay the warmup tax.
[05:48] Carlos: Security question — if we do private deployment, how does KMS/HSM key management work for token encryption at rest?
[05:56] Maya: for Private we integrate with customer KMS (AWS KMS, HashiCorp, HSM) and offer envelope encryption; we also support audit logs and SAML SSO. we'll schedule a security deep dive with our security engineer.
[06:08] Priya: can we get an NDA'd copy of the SOC2 artifact?
[06:11] Maya: yes i'll include the SOC2 summary and a pointer to the security whitepaper in the doc bundle.
[06:18] Carlos: back to sizing — if we map your 50 rps per GPU number, for our steady 120 rps we need 3 GPUs baseline. for 900 rps burst we need 18 GPUs. does that align?
[06:27] Ethan: yes roughly; with a hot pool of 3 and a burst pool that can spin to 18 you'd be covered. recommend adding 1-2 spare nodes for headroom and quantization tests.
[06:36] Ben: and does Redwood support heterogeneous pools? e.g. a mix of A10s and A100s?
[06:40] Ethan: yes you can define node groups with different instance types; routing will consider model-compatibility and latency. often teams put H100s for heavy batched offline jobs and A10/A100 for low-latency online.
[06:50] Priya: for the POC run, can you produce two concrete scenarios in the sheet: conservative (min-cost, higher latency at peak) and conservative-plus (higher cost, meets p95 targets)?
[06:58] Maya: yep, we'll prepare conservative and performance scenarios with explicit node counts, scale policies, and cost deltas.
[07:05] Carlos: and include guidance about max_batch_size and per-route timeouts please.
[07:09] Ethan: will do. also include a recommended canary for the rollout: 5% -> 25% -> 100% with a 15m observation window each.
[07:18] Priya: any gotchas with our k8s ingress? we use nginx-ingress and internal LB.
[07:23] Ethan: sounds fine, but ensure your internal LB supports connection drain and appropriate timeouts; long-lived streaming responses need sticky-ish behavior. we'll send nginx config snippets.
[07:33] Ben: curious about observability hooks: can we get token-level cost breakdowns per route?
[07:38] Maya: yes Redwood Console provides per-route token and latency breakdowns; we can enable additional retention for the POC.
[07:45] Carlos: ok great. sounds like the action items are clear.
[07:49] Maya: quick recap of next steps: we'll send the sizing spreadsheet + pricing delta + benchmark plan; Ethan will share bench plan; Nimbus will share traces; we'll propose security deep-dive times.
[07:59] Priya: thanks, i have one last quick ask — can Redwood run a short 2h benchmark that simulates our peakhour?
[08:06] Ethan: yes straight-forward — we'll coordinate on exact payloads. we'll aim to run it in our test cluster and share results.
[08:12] Carlos: perfect. thanks everyone.

End of call.
